name: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies

clinicalPearls: Caused most often by a deletion of the chromosome 17 region containing PMP22, the reciprocal rearrangement to the duplication that causes CMT1A; inheritance is autosomal dominant.
Presents with recurrent, painless, focal mononeuropathies precipitated by minor compression, stretch, trauma or repetitive movement.
Typical sites are the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head, the ulnar nerve at the elbow, the median nerve at the wrist and the brachial plexus.
Recovery from individual episodes is usually good, but may be incomplete, so deficits can accumulate over time.
Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing at entrapment and compression sites superimposed on a diffuse, often subclinical, background neuropathy.
Sural nerve biopsy shows tomacula, the sausage-shaped focal myelin thickenings that give the alternative name tomaculous neuropathy.
Diagnosis is confirmed by PMP22 deletion testing (for example MLPA); a minority of cases arise from PMP22 point mutations.
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies is most often caused by a deletion of the chromosome 17 region containing PMP22, the reciprocal rearrangement to the duplication responsible for CMT1A. Reduced PMP22 dosage (haploinsufficiency) leads to unstable, focally thickened myelin bearing characteristic sausage-shaped swellings (tomacula) and renders myelinated fibres abnormally vulnerable to mechanical stresses such as compression, stretch and repetitive movement. At sites of entrapment or external pressure this produces focal conduction block and demyelination, manifesting as acute, typically painless focal palsies superimposed on a diffuse and often subclinical background neuropathy that can be detected electrophysiologically. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and a minority of cases result from point mutations in PMP22 rather than from the deletion.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent ordinary entrapment neuropathies (carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow)
Multifocal motor neuropathy or multifocal acquired demyelinating neuropathy
Vasculitic neuropathy presenting as mononeuritis multiplex
Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome), though this is characteristically painful
CMT1A and other forms of CMT
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography (focal slowing at compression sites, prolonged distal latencies, diffuse background abnormality)
Sural nerve biopsy only if genetic testing is negative and the diagnosis remains unclear (tomacula)
Screening for reversible contributors such as diabetes or thyroid dysfunction that add to entrapment risk
redFlags: Painful mononeuritis multiplex, which points instead to a vasculitic neuropathy
Progressive, non-remitting deficits occurring without any compressive trigger
Rapidly evolving generalised weakness suggesting an inflammatory or alternative cause
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good, with most palsies recovering over weeks to months, although repeated episodes can leave residual deficits; lifespan is normal.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent palsies to isolated entrapment and missing the underlying hereditary cause.
Proceeding to decompressive surgery without recognising the underlying HNPP.
Advising activities or postures that provoke nerve compression, such as prolonged leg-crossing or leaning on the elbows.
Expecting pain, when HNPP palsies are characteristically painless.
management: Counsel patients to avoid compression, stretch and repetitive activity at vulnerable sites such as the common peroneal nerve at the fibular head, the ulnar nerve at the elbow and the median nerve at the wrist
Support focal palsies with physiotherapy, orthoses such as an ankle-foot orthosis or wrist splint, and occupational therapy
Manage neuropathic pain symptomatically where it occurs
Identify and treat reversible contributors that add to entrapment risk, such as diabetes mellitus or thyroid dysfunction
Take care to prevent iatrogenic compression during surgery, anaesthetic positioning and prolonged immobilisation, and reserve surgical decompression for selected cases
Monitor for accumulating residual deficits after recurrent episodes
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and PMP22 deletion testing of relatives
